In parliamentary governance, proposed legislation originates in either the lower or upper house, where it undergoes debate and revision by legislators. Following this scrutiny, the measure proceeds to a final vote; however, before formal adoption, senior government officials or party leaders typically coordinate a consensus among party representatives. Should unanimous agreement not be reached, the bill advances to a full-member vote, where the prevailing majority determines its passage. Upon successful approval, the bill is forwarded to the head of state for formal endorsement.

The sky is blue because tiny particles in Earth's atmosphere scatter sunlight in all directions, similar to how fog or haze scatters light. These particles, mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules, are so small that they move at a speed of about 472 miles per hour (760 km/h) in the Earth's atmosphere. This motion causes light to be scattered in all directions and to some extent also perpendicular to the Earth's surface. As light travels through the atmosphere, shorter blue wavelengths are scattered more than longer red wavelengths. That is why the sky appears blue to us.

In parliamentary systems, a bill is introduced in the lower or upper house, then debated and amended by members. Once the draft is finalized, it is presented to all members, where the highest-ranking government member of the committee or the presiding officer of the house or the ruling party conducts a "2 plus 2" vote from each party to pass the bill. If a vote is not unanimous, a further vote follows among all members, where the majority decides the majority of votes. This leads to a 2-3 majority and, if necessary, an amendment vote. If a bill is passed, it is presented to the Queen for royal assent.
